project.domain: humanitarian programme evidence and safeguarded workflow assistance

thesis: Programme evidence may inform a recommendation, but sensitive beneficiary context and external follow-up authority remain behind deterministic minimisation and human approval.

evidence.claim: External workflow effects are prepared by deterministic rules and cannot execute without explicit approval.
Least privilege and human authority are explicit design principles.
Automated steps prepare work without inheriting external execution authority.
The public proof is synthetic and does not claim production identity/RBAC or organisational tenancy.
Execution without approval is blocked and simulated execution occurs only after approval.
Programme claims are evaluated against explicit synthetic evidence fixtures and unsupported claims remain visible.
Sensitive-context minimisation and synthetic-data-only enforcement are regression-tested.
Safeguarding by design minimises sensitive context before downstream AI integration.
The demonstrated workflow has a bounded deterministic state machine and no autonomous external connector.
Organisation-approved LLM routing and production integration choices are explicitly future targets rather than present claims.
High-risk privacy/authority failure modes are tested, but there is not yet a dedicated prompt-injection/agentic red-team suite.
Production observability and security review are explicit future integration targets.

adversarial.taxonomy: No dedicated agentic-security gauntlet published yet

residualRisks: No dedicated adversarial prompt-injection or agentic-security suite is published yet.
Identity, RBAC, encrypted storage, retention and production observability are integration targets rather than proven controls in this static proof.
Real PII/NER classification and organisation-approved model routing require the actual deployment context.
The prototype is not an approved Plan International system and uses no real beneficiary data.
